title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Osaki Electric confirms data was stolen in the ransomware attack that halted three smart-meter plants, and plans a staged restart from 27 November
items.content_text: Osaki Electric, Japan’s largest smart-meter maker, confirmed on 17 November that ransomware had encrypted some of its virtual servers, and on 18 November it stopped production-related systems at Saitama Works and at group companies Iwate Osaki Electric and Osaki Platec, halting production and shipments. Its 20 November update said the intruder most likely got in on 15 November through a VPN device, by repeated password attempts on an account without multi-factor authentication. A 25 November filing confirms data was sent to an external destination and sets out a staged production restart from 27 November, with shipments planned from 1 and 7 December. Production equipment and installed meters are reported unaffected. Precautionary shutdowns like this are how ransomware usually stops a factory (editorial assessment).

items.title: Peninsula Energy confirms the attack on its Wyoming uranium project reached plant and wellfield control systems, and the site is shut down
items.content_text: Peninsula Energy, an ASX-listed uranium producer, said on 25 November that the cyberattack found on 20 November reached the plant and wellfield operating and control systems at its Lance in-situ recovery project in Crook County, Wyoming, and that the site has been shut down. Its first disclosure, on 23 November, said US and Australian administrative systems were not affected. The shares remain suspended until 30 November. The company has not named an attacker, said how the intruders got in or given a restart date, and no group has claimed the attack. For process manufacturers, it shows that an incident on the operating side forces a full stop unless a manual or safe-state mode has been rehearsed (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: An AI-assisted crew breached Check Point management servers at more than 20 organizations, manufacturers among them
items.content_text: GreyNoise reported, as covered by Cybersecurity Dive on 24 November, that a crew it tracks as GT13 used AI-assisted tooling to break into Check Point Security Management servers at no fewer than 22 organizations, including energy, transportation and manufacturing firms, between 17 October and 2 November. A management server holds the policy and administrator access for every gateway it controls, so one compromised server can open a path toward plant networks. Victims are not named and no OT impact has been reported. The activity is separate from the PHP2Shell gateway attacks in the card above, and it fits the UK NCSC’s warning that AI-assisted attackers are exploiting familiar weaknesses faster (editorial assessment).

items.title: AI-run intrusions took about 150,000 documents from an industrial-automation manufacturer and planted admin accounts at a chip maker, Unit 42 says
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 12 November that an actor it tracks as CL-STA-1238 ran 25 operations against at least 19 organizations in August and September using Cairn, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework, and confirmed access or data theft at 10. Seven targets were in semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chains. At an industrial-automation manufacturer the attackers accessed roughly 150,000 internal documents; at a semiconductor company they brute-forced a production credential shared across accounts on a partner-integration application, then created administrator accounts and a persistent API token. Entry relied on weak and shared passwords, authentication flaws and old CVEs. Unit 42 assesses with moderate confidence that this is China-nexus intelligence collection. No ICS compromise or production outage is reported; design and partner data are the prize (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost. Belgium’s interior minister said on 12 November that evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution; France has blamed Iran’s IRGC for its October attack, and a pro-Russian claim is unverified. Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. Cold-storage and process-cooling controllers in food, chemical and pharmaceutical plants face the same risk if reachable from the internet (editorial assessment).

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims rose from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 876 cases (69%), led by construction, equipment and food and beverage makers, with automotive at 53. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. For plants, the real question is how long production can run without corporate IT (editorial assessment).

items.title: Intel 471: manufacturing was the sector most targeted by ransomware groups and access brokers from January to October
items.content_text: Intel 471 said on 18 November that manufacturing was the sector most targeted by ransomware and extortion groups between January and October 2026, with 1,379 claimed victims, 16.8% of all the victims it tracked. Initial access brokers advertised access affecting 172 manufacturing entities, about 10% of all accesses offered for sale in the period. Perimeter remote access dominated those listings, with VPN access alone making up 28.5%. Intel 471 names Qilin, The Gentlemen and Akira among the groups most active against manufacturers and automotive supply chains. The figures come from Intel 471’s own tracking of leak sites and criminal forums and have not been independently verified. For plants, the practical point is that a working VPN login may already be on sale before anyone uses it (editorial assessment).

items.title: FBI warns that the ARTEX AI attack framework is reaching privileged access in under three hours, with manufacturing among its targets
items.content_text: The FBI issued a FLASH alert on 13 November about ARTEX, an open-source, AI-driven penetration-testing framework that multiple malicious actors have used since at least August 2026 to automate intrusions from reconnaissance to data theft. Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours. The FBI lists manufacturing, semiconductor, energy, telecommunications and other sectors as targets and counts more than 1,600 exposed ARTEX consoles as of early November; the original repository was removed in October, but forks and a commercial version persist. Its examples include attacks on South Korean financial institutions and the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise, which produced sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 downstream tenants. No controller compromise or OT outage is described. Faster intrusions shrink the time between a missed patch and a stopped plant (editorial assessment).

items.title: Switzerland confirms its first AI-agent cyberattacks: four of five succeeded, using weak passwords and known flaws in internet-facing systems
items.content_text: Switzerland’s Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS) said on 26 November that five attacks in recent days used AI agents, frameworks that find weaknesses, pick tools and plan their next steps largely on their own. Four of the five compromised systems. Three targets were critical-infrastructure operators, which public broadcaster SRF identified as electricity, water and telecommunications providers. BACS named no victims or attacker and has not said whether any control systems were reached. The entry points were ordinary: default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing systems. No manufacturer is named, but plants expose the same remote-access, HMI and vendor-support services, and the FBI’s ARTEX warning lists manufacturing among targets. AI is hitting old weaknesses faster, not inventing new ones (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: A CVSS 9.8 Brotli flaw reaches more than a dozen Siemens HMI, SCADA and engineering products, and most have no fix yet
items.content_text: Siemens advisory SSA-242944, republished by CISA on 17 November as ICSA-26-321-03, covers CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder (versions 1.0.3 to 1.2.0) linked to the Node.js “Node2Shell” fixes of 21 October. A remote, unauthenticated attacker sending a crafted Brotli-compressed stream could crash the service, leak memory or possibly run code; CVSS v3.1 is 9.8. Fixes exist only for SIMATIC Braumat and Sistar (V8.2 Update 5) and WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1). WinCC V7/V8, WinCC Runtime Professional, the WinCC Unified family, WinCC OA V3.21, TIA Administrator, User Management Component and COMOS Walkinside have no fix yet, and the SIMATIC Profiling Tool will get none. CISA lists the CVE in KEV because of attacks on other software; none aimed at Siemens products is reported.

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the cases Mandiant investigated, the group entered through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, attacked vCenter in early September, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: CISA says attackers are exploiting a year-old SAP NetWeaver flaw, putting the ERP layer many plants depend on in scope
items.content_text: CISA warned on 20 November that attackers are exploiting CVE-2025-42884 in SAP NetWeaver, adding it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog alongside the Cisco Expressway and vCenter flaws, SecurityWeek reported on 23 November. The medium-severity bug (CVSS 6.5) lets an unauthenticated attacker inject JNDI environment properties and reach an unintended JNDI provider, which can leak or change server information. SAP fixed it in its November 2025 security updates, and SecurityWeek found no earlier public report of exploitation. Attackers and victims are not named. Many manufacturers run production orders, material planning and shipping through SAP, and Dragos counts ERP outages among the main reasons ransomware stops plants, so an unpatched NetWeaver server is a production risk even though it sits on the IT side (editorial assessment).

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Separately, on 20 November N-able said attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud; it reports no access to customer data and no link to N-central. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment).

items.title: Siemens: an NTLM relay flaw in PCS 7, WinCC and Process Historian will not be fixed in older versions, and opening a WinCC graphics file can run code
items.content_text: Two Siemens advisories republished by CISA on 17 November reach the core of many process and discrete plants. CVE-2026-58114 (CVSS v3.1 7.5) lets an unauthenticated attacker in a machine-in-the-middle position relay NTLM authentication and impersonate a user, for example against the SQL server WinCC uses. It affects SIMATIC PCS 7 V9.1, Batch V9.1, Information Server and Process Historian 2020 and 2022, for which no fix is planned, and WinCC V7.5 to V8.1 and WinCC Runtime Professional V17 to V21, which have no fix yet. Separately, CVE-2026-59082 (CVSS 7.8) in the WinCC Graphics Designer can run code when a user opens a malicious file; there is no fix for V7.5, V8.0 or V8.1. Neither flaw is reported exploited.

items.title: A booby-trapped project file can run code on engineering laptops through AutomationDirect’s C-More EA9 HMI programming software
items.content_text: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-328-01 on 24 November for AutomationDirect’s C-More EA9 programming software, the Windows tool used to build screens for C-More EA9 touch-panel HMIs. CVE-2026-127280, rated CVSS 7.8, is a heap-based buffer overflow: opening a maliciously crafted project file in version 6.80 or earlier could let an attacker run code on the engineering workstation. CISA lists critical manufacturing, energy and water among the affected sectors and reports no known exploitation. Because a user has to open the file, the realistic risk is a tampered project arriving by email, a shared drive or a contractor’s USB stick. AutomationDirect HMIs are common at small and mid-size plants and machine builders (editorial assessment).

items.title: Schneider fixes a project-file flaw in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody, the switchboard design tool used by panel builders
items.content_text: CISA republished Schneider Electric’s advisory on 24 November as ICSA-26-328-02, covering EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody, the Windows software panel builders and electrical contractors use to design and quote low-voltage switchboards. CVE-2026-119055 is a use-after-free in how the tool handles SSD project files: if a user opens a crafted file on the local machine, the application could crash or, in the worst case, run code. Schneider rates it Medium (CVSS v4 4.6, v3.1 5.3) and published fixed builds for each language version, for example 2.9.12.0101 for the French release and 2.9.5.0000 for the Spanish release, in its 10 November notice. No exploitation is reported. It is a low-priority patch, but design laptops that swap project files with customers deserve the same care as engineering workstations (editorial assessment).

items.title: UK NCSC says AI-assisted attackers are exploiting familiar weaknesses faster, and urges organizations to shrink what they expose
items.content_text: The UK National Cyber Security Centre said in a 24 November blog that since September it has seen a rise in AI-assisted, “agentic” attacks that exploit familiar weaknesses in internet-facing services, shortening the time defenders have to react. Its guidance centres on reducing exposure: knowing which services face the internet, removing the ones that do not need to, and fixing known weaknesses on the rest quickly. The blog is guidance and creates no new obligations. It lines up with the FBI’s ARTEX warning and GreyNoise’s GT13 report on this page; for plants, it argues for taking exposed HMI, remote-desktop and vendor-access services off the internet rather than relying on patch speed alone (editorial assessment).

items.title: Critical-infrastructure CEOs, now including manufacturers, are told to answer four recovery questions within 30 days as AI speeds up attacks
items.content_text: The Alliance for Critical Infrastructure, a trade association launched in February 2026, issued guidance to chief executives on AI-accelerated cyber risk, reported by Cybersecurity Dive on 25 November. It has added CEOs from six sectors, including manufacturing, chemical and food and agriculture, bringing its representation to 12 of the 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors. It asks leaders to be able to answer four questions within 30 days: which systems they cannot lose, how quickly they can respond to a serious threat, whether recovery has been verified, and who owns risk on systems that cannot be patched. It also urges reviewing internet exposure, disconnecting unneeded devices, governing agentic AI and testing recovery plans. The guidance is voluntary, but the four questions make a useful plant-level board brief (editorial assessment).

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of SP 800-82, the OT security guide many plant audits are measured against
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions and applying zero-trust principles. Customers, insurers and auditors often use 800-82 as a reference for manufacturers, so its final wording can shape what plants are asked to show; the comment window is the chance to flag guidance that would not work on a production floor (editorial assessment).
